notes: A contested claim: single-laboratory description, not widely replicated, and the supporting evidence is weak.

mechanism: Nuclear FOXO1 drives the hepatic gluconeogenic transcriptional programme; AKT-dependent exclusion is how insulin suppresses glucose output.
Glucokinase phosphorylates glucose to glucose-6-phosphate, committing hepatic glucose to glycolytic flux.
Insulin and IGF-1 receptor engagement activates class I PI3K through IRS proteins, generating the PIP3 signal upstream of mTORC2.
SGK1-driven distal nephron sodium reabsorption sustains extracellular volume and blood pressure; its failure produces salt wasting and hypotension.
Rictor deletion impairs long-term memory alongside L-LTP while sparing short-term memory.
An acidic loop of the mSin1 CRIM domain engages the basic AKT N-lobe surface ~75 Å from the catalytic site, encoding substrate choice by distal docking rather than local sequence.
notes: Residues flanking Ser473 are unimportant for phosphorylation. The same N-lobe residues engage phospho-Thr450, so AKT must change conformation first, which builds a proofreading step into substrate selection. The distal-docking geometry rests on a single structural study.

mechanism: mSin1 contributes with Rictor to occlusion of the FRB domain in assembled mTORC2.

In the basal state the mSin1 PH domain folds back onto the mTOR kinase domain and autoinhibits mTORC2. PIP3 binding to the PH domain relieves this autoinhibition and recruits the complex to the plasma membrane.
notes: Reproduced across laboratories.

mechanism: mSin1 binds Rictor through its N-terminal segment and maintains Rictor–mTOR complex integrity; its loss abolishes AKT Ser473 phosphorylation.
mSin1 CRIM-dependent recruitment of AGC kinases extends to protein kinase C isoforms; mTORC2 substrate preference among AGC kinases is modulated by subtle Rictor-mSin1 interface changes.
notes: Graded emerging rather than established: [74] demonstrates Sin1-dependent recruitment of AGC kinases, but isoform-resolved dependence of each PKC on mSin1 is less completely shown than for AKT and SGK1.

mechanism: The central CRIM domain of mSin1 recruits AGC-kinase substrates generally, not AKT alone; Sin1-dependent recruitment is required for mTORC2 to phosphorylate SGK1, and different AGC kinases are differentially sensitive to perturbation of mSin1.
notes: The SGK1 and PKC arms are missing.

mechanism: mSin1 splice isoforms assemble distinct mTORC2 species; the isoform lacking the C-terminal PH domain yields a complex not gated by PIP3.
notes: Alternative splicing of mSin1 generates three mTORC2 species; the assignment comes from a single biochemical study and has not been independently reproduced, although the behaviour of the complex built on the isoform lacking the C-terminal PH domain is consistent with later work showing that the PH domain autoinhibits the complex until PIP3 binds.

mechanism: AKT phosphorylates MDM2 and promotes its nuclear translocation, where it drives p53 ubiquitination and degradation, removing p53-dependent apoptotic and cell-cycle-arrest output.
notes: Whether this substrate depends on AKT hydrophobic-motif phosphorylation has not been tested.

mechanism: mLST8 contacts the kinase domain near the activation loop and stabilises the catalytic conformation.
WD40 β-propeller abutting the kinase domain near the activation loop
ChREBP activates glucose-responsive lipogenic transcription in adipocytes.
Two mTOR protomers form the catalytic core of the ~1.0 MDa mTORC2 homodimer, resolved by cryo-EM at 3.2 Å.
mTOR is the catalytic subunit of the putative ETV7-containing mTORC3 assembly.
notes: keeps mTORC3 connected to the catalytic tier.

mechanism: Control of the actin cytoskeleton was the founding mTORC2 phenotype, defined by the rapamycin-insensitive, raptor-independent Rictor–mTOR complex.
Turn-motif phosphorylation at Thr450 is constitutive and occurs cotranslationally on ribosome-associated mTORC2; it is required for folding and stability of nascent AKT.
notes: Phospho-Thr450 is also read by the mSin1 CRIM docking surface, coupling stability to the Ser473 proofreading step [597].

mechanism: mTORC2 is the hydrophobic-motif (PDK2) kinase for AKT; with PDK1-mediated Thr308 it gives full AKT activity.
notes: Identification of mTORC2 as the long-sought PDK2 resolved more than a decade of uncertainty.

mechanism: Ser473 phosphorylation markedly enhances AKT activity toward BAD, biasing mTORC2 output toward survival signalling.
notes: Ser473-dependent substrate selectivity has been demonstrated for FOXO1 and FOXO3a in cells lacking mTORC2 components; its extension to BAD is inferred rather than directly shown.

mechanism: Loss of mTORC2 in beta-cells lowers AKT Ser473 phosphorylation and permits nuclear FOXO1 accumulation, with a consequent rise in p27 protein and reduced beta-cell mass; the step is indirect and was scored at the protein level.
notes: Transcriptional and post-translational routes to p27 accumulation were not distinguished.

mechanism: By supplying Ser473, mTORC2 biases AKT output toward survival and transcriptional programmes (FOXO, BAD) rather than toward its metabolic substrates.
Active mTOR phosphorylates its own inhibitory subunit DEPTOR, marking it for degradation — a self-amplifying loop in which active mTOR removes its own brake.

Ser473 phosphorylation is substrate-selective rather than globally activating: AKT phosphorylated only at Thr308 retains substantial activity toward GSK3-beta and TSC2, whereas Ser473 markedly enhances activity toward FOXO1. mTORC2 therefore specifically suppresses FOXO1.
notes: Ref [204] (Guertin 2006) is titled 'mTORC2 is required for signaling to Akt-FOXO' and is direct support.

mechanism: Ser473 phosphorylation markedly enhances AKT activity toward FOXO3a, so mTORC2 loss de-represses FOXO3a-dependent transcription.
Hepatic mTORC2 supports glycolysis through AKT-dependent glucokinase expression.
Hepatic mTORC2, acting through AKT-mediated FOXO1 suppression, restrains gluconeogenesis; liver-specific Rictor deletion produces glucose intolerance.
notes: Opposite in sign to hepatic mTORC1 output, which is the basis of the complex-divergence argument for liver.

mechanism: Adipocyte Rictor deletion reduces insulin-stimulated glucose uptake; mTORC2 output through AKT is the limiting arm.

The intrinsic tyrosine kinase activity of mTOR within mTORC2 has been reported to phosphorylate and activate the type I IGF receptor and the insulin receptor, constituting a feed-forward arm from mTORC2 back onto the receptor tier that would amplify PI3K-PIP3 input to mTORC2 itself.
notes: Graded emerging: the claim that mTOR has tyrosine kinase activity is not independently replicated as widely as the serine/threonine activity and should not be presented as settled.

mechanism: Insulin secretion and beta-cell survival depend on mTORC2 in the islet, so both complexes are required there, unlike the opposing arrangement in liver and adipose tissue; reduced insulin output contributes to the dysglycaemia seen at immunosuppressive exposures of mTOR inhibitors.
notes: Beta-cell Rictor deletion principally reduces beta-cell mass and proliferation, and the fall in insulin output has not been dissociated from that loss of mass.

mechanism: Lipolysis and insulin-stimulated glucose uptake are the adipose outputs that depend on mTORC2; adipocyte Rictor deletion alters lipid handling, and pharmacological inhibition is expected to produce altered lipid handling and hypertriglyceridaemia.
Forebrain Rictor deletion selectively impairs L-LTP while leaving early-phase LTP intact; mTORC1 supports the translational component, mTORC2 the structural one.
notes: Reproduced across laboratories.

mechanism: A distinct mTORC2–AKT pool resides at ER–mitochondria contact sites and controls MAM integrity, Ca2+ transfer and mitochondrial physiology.
notes: Reported by a single laboratory and not independently replicated.

mechanism: Adipose mTORC2 drives ChREBP-dependent de novo lipogenesis, with consequences for hepatic glucose metabolism.

mTOR autophosphorylates at Ser2481 within the assembled complex; in mTORC2 this autophosphorylation is a complex-specific readout of intrinsic catalytic activity and is rapamycin-insensitive under acute treatment, unlike the mTORC1-associated pool.
notes: Ser2481 is an activity-associated readout; the cited study does not establish that phosphorylation at this site activates mTOR.

mechanism: Oligodendrocyte-lineage Rictor deletion has modest and largely transient effects on myelination, whereas Raptor loss causes persistent hypomyelination; only the raptor/rictor double mutant impairs oligodendrocyte differentiation itself, indicating that mTORC2 contributes but is not rate-limiting while mTORC1 remains intact.
context: rodent; regional - spinal cord affected more than corpus callosum
notes: Effect is 'modulates', not 'required_for': the cited work shows mTORC2 is explicitly NOT rate-limiting. Encoding this as a requirement would misrepresent the source.

mechanism: A small molecule that raises mTORC2 activity reverses age-associated long-term memory impairment in aged mice and flies, and enhancing mTORC2-dependent actin polymerisation likewise improves long-term memory.
notes: Pharmacological gain-of-function evidence from a single report in mice and flies, with no independent replication and no human data.

mechanism: mTORC2 in adipose tissue negatively controls whole-body growth, so adipocyte Rictor deletion increases body size - a direction of effect opposite to the usual anabolic framing of the pathway.
notes: Ref [126] (Cybulski 2009) is titled 'mTOR complex 2 in adipose tissue negatively controls whole-body growth'.

mechanism: Loss of mTORC2 removes AKT-dependent FOXO1 suppression and insulin-stimulated glucose uptake, producing glucose intolerance and peripheral insulin resistance.
Renal mTORC2 loss causes salt wasting and hypotension through failure of SGK1-dependent activation of ENaC, the Na+/K+-ATPase and CLC-K in the distal nephron.

Chronic mTORC2 loss produces peripheral insulin resistance, which is distinct from direct beta-cell toxicity; the two together account for new-onset diabetes after transplantation at immunosuppressive exposures.

Conditional Rictor deletion in the postnatal murine forebrain selectively impairs long-term memory while sparing short-term memory; conversely, a compound that raises mTORC2 activity converts early-phase into late-phase potentiation, enhances long-term memory in wild-type animals and reverses age-associated memory impairment in mice and flies.
notes: The requirement is bidirectional and pharmacologically accessible, which is what underlies concern about cognitive effects of inhibitors that reach mTORC2.

mechanism: Renal mTORC2 loss abolishes SGK1-dependent ENaC and Na+/K+-ATPase regulation, causing salt wasting and hypotension.
Spine density falls when forebrain mTORC2 activity and Tiam1–Rac1-dependent actin polymerisation are reduced.
mTORC2 primes selected PKC isoforms for maturation; PDK1 phosphorylation and hydrophobic-motif autophosphorylation follow.
A PIP3-gated pool of mTORC2 operates at the plasma membrane, where AKT is recruited by the same lipid.
mTORC2-dependent priming supports maturation of this PKC isoform. Hydrophobic-motif phosphorylation is not assigned as a direct mTORC2 reaction.
mTORC2-dependent priming supports maturation of this PKC isoform. Hydrophobic-motif phosphorylation is not assigned as a direct mTORC2 reaction.
mTORC2 phosphorylates the turn and hydrophobic motifs of the novel isoform PKCδ, supporting its stability and migration signalling.
notes: Specific residue numbers not asserted. Bibliographic details given External reference not independently verified.

mechanism: PKCε is among the novel PKC isoforms whose mTORC2-dependent priming-site phosphorylation is required for maturation and stability.
notes: Isoform-level data are thinner than for PKCα; residues not asserted.

mechanism: mTORC2 phosphorylates the turn motif of the atypical isoform PKCζ, regulating its stability and activity.
notes: Residue number not asserted. Bibliographic details given External reference not independently verified.

mechanism: mTORC2 phosphorylates the SGK1 hydrophobic motif, which is required for SGK1 activity.

Hepatic mTORC2 supports lipogenesis through SREBP1c and glycolysis through glucokinase; the effect on SREBP1c is relayed by AKT and no direct action of the complex on the transcription factor has been shown.

Rictor-mTORC2 is required for Th2 differentiation, whereas Rheb-mTORC1 is required for Th1 and Th17; both complexes are additionally required for the glycolytic and glutaminolytic reprogramming of effector activation.
Conditional Rictor deletion in the postnatal forebrain lowers Tiam1 levels and Tiam1-dependent Rac1 activation; the step between the complex and Tiam1 is undefined.
notes: Tiam1 is not a known substrate of the complex, and the relationship rests on a single line of work in one tissue.

mechanism: Adipocyte Rictor deletion reduces insulin-stimulated glucose uptake, alters lipid handling and negatively controls whole-body growth.
β-cell Rictor deletion causes mild hyperglycaemia with reduced β-cell mass, decreased AKT Ser473 phosphorylation, nuclear FOXO1 accumulation and elevated p27.

Conditional deletion of Rictor in the postnatal murine forebrain reduces mTORC2 activity and selectively impairs late-phase long-term potentiation and long-term memory while sparing early-phase potentiation and short-term memory; the mechanism is Tiam1–Rac1-dependent actin polymerisation with reduced dendritic spine density, and raising mTORC2 activity pharmacologically enhances long-term memory and reverses its age-associated decline.
notes: The rodent genetics are well supported; the inference that this creates a cognitive deficit missed by standard metabolic monitoring, and its extrapolation to chronic low-dose human dosing, are not.

mechanism: Cardiomyocyte mTORC2 limits apoptosis and tissue loss after ischaemic injury through AKT-dependent anti-apoptotic signalling, complementing the mTORC1 contribution to physiological growth, so agents that ablate both complexes are predicted to be more cardiotoxic than mTORC1-selective ones.
notes: Shown in a myocardial infarction model in which suppression of mTORC2 increased cardiomyocyte apoptosis and tissue damage.

mechanism: mTORC2-dependent SGK1 activity governs ion handling in the distal nephron and therefore sodium balance and blood pressure; renal mTORC2 loss causes salt wasting and hypotension.
Hepatic mTORC2 restrains gluconeogenesis and supports glycolysis and lipogenesis; liver-specific Rictor deletion gives a type-2-diabetes-like phenotype.
mTORC2 contributes to oligodendrocyte differentiation but is not rate-limiting while mTORC1 is intact; the deficit becomes apparent only in the raptor/rictor double mutant.

Muscle-specific Rictor deletion is close to phenotypically silent, in contrast to Raptor deletion, which causes dystrophy; the residual mTORC2 contribution is limited to loss of AKT Ser473 phosphorylation and a modest fall in insulin-stimulated glucose uptake.
notes: Negative result, retained because the asymmetry between the complexes in muscle is what predicts the tissue's drug response.

mechanism: mTORC2 supports Th2 effector differentiation and AKT-dependent survival in T lymphocytes; with mTORC1 it governs the metabolic reprogramming of effector activation and restrains Treg commitment.

Loss of total mTOR kinase activity abrogates Th1, Th2 and Th17 differentiation and favours Foxp3 induction, which underlies the preferential expansion of regulatory T cells under rapamycin; restraint of regulatory T cell differentiation is best documented for the AKT–mTORC1 arm, while deletion of Rictor alone has smaller and less consistent effects.
notes: Both complexes have been reported to restrain regulatory T cell differentiation, but loss of mTORC2 alone can leave suppressive function intact or even improved. This is the one tissue setting in which the consequence of inhibition is the desired therapeutic effect rather than a toxicity.

sites: N-terminal cytoplasmic lysines of the ENaC subunits
mechanism: The WW domains of Nedd4-2 bind PY motifs in the cytoplasmic C-termini of the ENaC subunits, and the ligase conjugates ubiquitin to lysines in their N-terminal tails, driving channel retrieval and degradation and lowering apical sodium conductance.
PDK1 phosphorylates the AKT activation loop; AKT requires this together with Ser473 for full activity.

Growth-factor signalling through PI3K has been reported to promote association of mTORC2 with the ribosome as an activating input; this step comes from a single line of work, while the reproduced growth-factor input is direct PIP3 binding to the mSin1 PH domain, which relieves autoinhibition and recruits the complex to the membrane.
notes: Upstream control of mTORC2 beyond PIP3 binding and ribosome association remains poorly resolved.

mechanism: Class I PI3K, activated by receptor tyrosine kinase engagement, converts PIP2 to PIP3.
PIP3 recruits AKT to the plasma membrane through its PH domain, which is prerequisite for both Thr308 and Ser473 phosphorylation.
PIP3 binds the mSin1 PH domain and releases it from mTOR, relieving autoinhibition of the kinase.
notes: Reproduced across laboratories; the best-supported upstream input to mTORC2.

mechanism: PIP3 binding simultaneously recruits mTORC2 to the plasma membrane, co-localising it with its membrane-targeted substrate AKT.
Loss of mTORC2-primed PKC protein produces cytoskeletal defects, the mechanistic link between mTORC2 and actin organisation.
PKC-dependent Rho-family signalling supports adhesion dynamics, which fail when mTORC2 priming is lost.
Reduced PKC protein in mTORC2-deficient cells impairs migration.
mTORC2-dependent PKC activity is required for epithelial apicobasal polarity; mTORC2-deficient cells show polarity defects.

Loss of mTORC2 lowers PKC protein and activity and reduces Rho-family signalling, of which Rac1 is a member; a direct action of PKC on Rac1, plausibly through Rac guanine-nucleotide exchange factors, has not been established, and Rac1 has also been reported to act upstream of mTOR.
notes: Inferred from the cytoskeletal phenotype of mTORC2-deficient cells rather than from a defined molecular step.

mechanism: mTORC2-deficient cells lose PKC protein and show Rho-pathway and actomyosin defects; the connection from PKC to RhoA is inferred from this phenotype rather than demonstrated as a direct activating step.
notes: Inferred from the cytoskeletal phenotype of mTORC2-deficient cells rather than from a defined molecular step.

mechanism: Atypical PKC activity within the Par3–Par6–aPKC module specifies the apical domain by phosphorylating Par3, Lgl and Par1; PKC-iota/lambda and PKC-zeta act redundantly in mammalian epithelia, and their mTORC2-dependent stability links the complex to polarity.
notes: PKC-iota/lambda is the predominant atypical PKC in mammalian epithelia and acts redundantly with PKC-zeta.

mechanism: Protor-1 binds Rictor as a substoichiometric accessory subunit of mTORC2.
Protor-1 is required for efficient mTORC2-mediated SGK1 activation, an effect most evident in kidney.
notes: Protor-1/2 are implicated in SGK1 regulation.

mechanism: Protor-2 binds Rictor as a substoichiometric accessory subunit of mTORC2.

Protor-2 acts within mTORC2 to restrain phosphorylation of PKC-delta by the complex; its degradation downstream of G-alpha-12 permits PKC-delta phosphorylation and promotes cell migration, with no evidence of direct binding to the kinase.
PTEN dephosphorylates PIP3 to PIP2, terminating the lipid signal that relieves mSin1 autoinhibition and recruits mTORC2 and AKT.
Rac1·GTP drives branched actin polymerisation in dendritic spines.
Prolonged rapamycin exposure inhibits mTORC2 because FKBP12–rapamycin captures newly synthesised mTOR before assembly; mTORC1 selectivity is kinetic, not absolute.
Chronic rapamycin exposure disrupts mTORC2 and causes insulin resistance, an effect uncoupled from its longevity benefit.
notes: Whether intermittent dosing, which allows mTORC2 to recover between doses, spares glucose metabolism remains unsettled; the supporting evidence is preliminary [12].

mechanism: A minor subset of mTORC2 associates with ribosomes; this association activates the complex and provides a growth-factor-responsive input.
The AKT C-lobe engages an N-terminal mooring formed jointly by mSin1 and Rictor, completing the bipartite docking that positions Ser473 at the active site.
notes: A docking surface remote from the catalytic cleft is in principle a druggable site for genuinely mTORC2-selective inhibitors, which do not presently exist. Rests on the single 2025 structural study [597].

mechanism: Rictor packs against the FRB domain, occluding the FKBP12–rapamycin binding surface; this is the structural basis for rapamycin insensitivity of preassembled mTORC2.
Rictor is the defining subunit that distinguishes mTORC2 from mTORC1 and is raptor-independent.
S6K1-dependent mSin1 Thr86/Thr398 phosphorylation was reported to disrupt mTORC2 and reduce AKT Ser473 phosphorylation.
notes: Liu et al. reported negative regulation involving Thr86/Thr398; Yang et al. reported positive AKT-dependent regulation specifically at Thr86.

mechanism: mTORC1-activated S6K1 directly phosphorylates Rictor at Thr1135, creating a 14-3-3 binding site without altering mTORC2 assembly or in vitro kinase activity. Two studies found that a T1135A mutant raises AKT Ser473 phosphorylation, indicating feedback inhibition, whereas two others saw no major change in mTORC2 activity or AKT phosphorylation.
notes: Boulbès et al. 2010 [53] detected Thr1135 phosphorylation in mTORC2-deficient cells, suggesting that it may also regulate functions of Rictor outside mTORC2.

mechanism: ENaC provides the rate-limiting apical entry step for sodium reabsorption in the aldosterone-sensitive distal nephron.

SGK1 signalling increases Na+/K+-ATPase activity and surface abundance, maintaining the basolateral gradient for transepithelial sodium transport; the alpha1 subunit has not been shown to be a direct substrate of the kinase.

Coexpression of SGK1 increases CLC-K/barttin chloride channel activity in heterologous systems, which would complete the transcellular salt transport route; phosphorylation of the channel or of barttin has not been demonstrated.

SGK1 phosphorylates FOXO3a at Thr32 and Ser315, promoting 14-3-3 binding and nuclear exclusion. SGK1 and AKT phosphorylate overlapping but non-identical sites, so SGK1 provides a parallel, AKT-independent route from mTORC2 to FOXO suppression.
notes: The SGK1 arm matters because it is the reason SGK1 inhibition is not functionally redundant with AKT inhibition.

mechanism: SGK1 phosphorylates NDRG1, the standard cellular readout of mTORC2–SGK1 pathway activity.
notes: Bibliographic details given External reference not independently verified.

mechanism: SGK1 phosphorylates Nedd4-2, creating 14-3-3 binding sites that prevent it from ubiquitinating ENaC.
notes: Residue numbers not asserted. Bibliographic details given External reference not independently verified.

mechanism: SGK1 raises ENaC surface expression and open probability chiefly indirectly, by phosphorylating Nedd4-2 and relieving ubiquitin-dependent channel retrieval; direct phosphorylation of the channel alpha subunit has been reported in heterologous expression systems and may contribute to the rise in open probability.
SGK1 phosphorylates TSC2 at a site overlapping the AKT site, relieving TSC complex GAP activity toward Rheb and sustaining mTORC1 activity independently of AKT.
GLUT4 translocation to the plasma membrane is the proximate step in insulin-stimulated glucose uptake.
SREBP1c induces the lipogenic gene programme (FASN, ACC, SCD1).
AS160 GAP activity keeps its Rab substrates GDP-loaded and retains GLUT4 vesicles intracellularly until AKT phosphorylation relieves it.
notes: GAP polarity: negative regulator of GLUT4 translocation. External reference not independently verified.

mechanism: Tiam1 is a Rac1-specific GEF, loading Rac1 with GTP; GEF polarity is positive.
The TSC1–TSC2 complex physically associates with mTORC2 and promotes its activity toward AKT, independently of its Rheb GAP function.
notes: Polarity is opposite to the TSC-mTORC1 relationship.

mechanism: 14-3-3 dimers bind FOXO1 after AKT phosphorylates it at Thr24 and Ser256 (binding needs both sites). Binding impairs DNA binding and shifts FOXO1 to the cytoplasm, contributing to insulin- and growth factor-induced silencing of FOXO1 target genes.
notes: 14-3-3 is one of several redundant routes for FOXO1 nuclear exclusion; Ser319-cluster phosphorylation and leucine-rich export signals also act. In HEK293 cells, overexpressed FOXO1 was excluded from the nucleus after IGF-1 stimulation without 14-3-3 binding.

mechanism: Phosphorylation of FOXO3a by AKT or SGK1 creates 14-3-3 binding sites; 14-3-3 binding drives nuclear exclusion and cytoplasmic retention, terminating FOXO3a-dependent transcription.
notes: FOXO3 is a Ser473-selective AKT substrate.

mechanism: SGK1 phosphorylation of NEDD4-2 creates 14-3-3 binding sites; 14-3-3 binding sequesters the ligase away from ENaC, preventing PY-motif ubiquitination and increasing channel surface density.
S6K1-phosphorylated Thr1135 of Rictor recruits 14-3-3 proteins to Rictor and mTORC2. Whether this binding restrains mTORC2 signalling to AKT is unresolved.
notes: A Thr1135Ala Rictor mutant increased AKT Ser473 phosphorylation in two studies, whereas phospho-site mutants left mTORC2 kinase activity or AKT phosphorylation unchanged in two others.

mechanism: AMPK phosphorylates CRY1, promoting FBXL3-dependent ubiquitination and degradation; this destabilises the clock's negative limb and entrains the oscillator to cellular energy state.
context: mouse liver and fibroblasts; energy stress
notes: Lamia 2009 reported Ser71 as the destabilising site, with a second site also described. PMID 19833968 (Science 2009;326(5951):437-440).

mechanism: AMPK phosphorylates casein kinase 1ε at Ser389, increasing its activity toward PER2; a second route (besides CRY1) by which cellular energy status reaches the clock
notes: External identifier requires independent verification.

mechanism: Rhythmically phosphorylated BMAL1 associates with the cap-binding machinery and promotes cap-dependent translation, which would confer a circadian rhythm on bulk protein synthesis independently of its transcriptional output.
notes: Reported by one laboratory and not yet independently replicated; rhythmic mTORC1 activity could by itself account for the rhythm in protein synthesis.

mechanism: BMAL1 is the obligate bHLH-PAS partner of CLOCK; the heterodimer is the DNA-binding unit that drives E-box transcription.
S6K1-phosphorylated BMAL1 associates with the cap-binding translation machinery, acting as a rhythmic accessory factor at eIF4F rather than only as a transcription factor.
context: mouse liver, cap-binding and polysome fractions
notes: Reported in Lipton 2015; whether the contact with eIF4E is direct, and its stoichiometry, are not settled.

mechanism: BMAL1 acts as a negative regulator of mTORC1; Bmal1-null tissues show elevated mTORC1 activity, placing the clock's positive limb upstream of the kinase.
notes: The intermediates between BMAL1 and mTORC1 are not fully defined.

mechanism: Restricted feeding is the dominant entraining cue for peripheral oscillators, shifting the phase of hepatic circadian gene expression by up to twelve hours while leaving the suprachiasmatic clock unchanged, and caloric restriction likewise reprograms hepatic clock gene expression.

Caloric restriction lowers hepatic mTORC1 activity at some times of day while having no effect, or the opposite effect, at others, so the measured response depends on when liver is sampled relative to the feeding schedule.
notes: Based on a single study sampling mouse liver at six times across the day; dietary-restriction studies using different feeding schedules are therefore not directly comparable.

mechanism: C/EBPβ binds and activates autophagy gene promoters, generating the daily rhythm of autophagic flux in liver
Autophagic and lysosomal flux are under circadian control, so the magnitude of any mTORC1-dependent autophagy readout depends on sampling time — a confounder rarely addressed.
notes: Rhythmic autophagic and lysosomal flux is documented in the primary literature: PMID 21897364 (Ma D, Panda S, Lin JD, 'Temporal orchestration of circadian autophagy rhythm by C/EBPbeta', EMBO J 2011;30(22):4642-4651).

mechanism: The clock imposes a daily rhythm on translation initiation and ribosome biogenesis, including rhythmic TOP mRNA translation driven by rhythmic mTORC1–S6K1 activity and by S6K1-phosphorylated BMAL1
notes: PMID corrected from 23300385 (an unrelated PLoS Biol neuroimaging paper) to 23300384, verified against PubMed as Jouffe C et al., 'The circadian clock coordinates ribosome biogenesis', PLoS Biol 2013;11(1):e1001455.

mechanism: Rhythmic expression of C/EBPβ is one clock output that times the hepatic autophagy gene programme

mTORC1 activity is itself rhythmic: PER2-dependent restraint operates in a time-of-day-dependent manner and the response of hepatic mTOR signalling to caloric restriction varies with time of day, so any mTORC1-dependent readout depends on sampling time
notes: Methodological consequence: the time of day at which samples are taken affects measured mTORC1 activity.

mechanism: S6K1 phosphorylation and downstream ribosome biogenesis oscillate over the day in liver, so mTORC1 output is itself a rhythmic variable rather than a constant baseline.
context: mouse liver, polysome and ribosome profiling
notes: PMID corrected from 23620741 (an unrelated PLoS One HIV capsid paper) to 23300384, verified against PubMed as Jouffe C et al., 'The circadian clock coordinates ribosome biogenesis', PLoS Biol 2013;11(1):e1001455.

mechanism: Feeding- and clock-driven rhythms in mTORC1 activity impose a daily rhythm on TFEB/TFE3 nuclear translocation, coupling the lysosomal–autophagic programme to time of day
notes: PMID corrected from 30988016 (which is Maslon MM, EMBO J 2019;38(9), a different paper in the same journal and year) to 31126958, verified against PubMed as Pastore N et al., 'Nutrient-sensitive transcription factors TFEB and TFE3 couple autophagy and metabolism to the peripheral clock', EMBO J 2019;38(12):e101347.

mechanism: CLOCK heterodimerises with BMAL1 through their PAS domains to form the positive-limb transcription factor of the mammalian oscillator.
CLOCK–BMAL1 drives E-box-dependent transcription of Cry1, which then returns to repress the heterodimer — the core delayed negative feedback loop.
Ddit4 (REDD1), a TSC-dependent inhibitor of mTORC1, is rhythmically expressed in mouse peripheral tissues, offering a candidate transcriptional route from the clock to mTORC1 restraint.
context: mouse peripheral tissues, circadian transcriptome atlas
notes: Rhythmic Ddit4 expression is documented in circadian transcriptome datasets (PMID 25349387: Zhang R et al., PNAS 2014;111(45):16219-16224), but that reference supports rhythmicity only: direct CLOCK-BMAL1 occupancy at the locus is not established and the glucocorticoid rhythm is an alternative driver, hence the emerging grading. Sestrin rhythmicity is not well documented.

mechanism: CLOCK–BMAL1 drives rhythmic transcription of Nr1d1 (Rev-erbα) through E-boxes, initiating the accessory stabilising loop
CLOCK–BMAL1 heterodimer binds E-boxes in the Per1 promoter and drives its rhythmic transcription
CLOCK–BMAL1 binds E-boxes in the Per2 promoter to drive its rhythmic transcription, generating the PER2 oscillation that times TSC1 recruitment to mTORC1.
CRY1 binds the CLOCK–BMAL1 heterodimer on DNA and blocks its transactivation, closing the negative limb of the feedback loop.
CRY1 is the repressive subunit of the PER–CRY complex; PER proteins control its nuclear entry and stability
CK1ε phosphorylation creates the phosphodegron that targets PER2 for ubiquitin-dependent degradation, shortening PER2 half-life and advancing clock phase
Hyperactivity reported alongside sleep–wake disturbance and hyperphagia as a recognised feature of the extended Smith–Kingsmore phenotype

Hyperphagia emerged as a recognised feature in a cohort of 28 individuals carrying nine pathogenic MTOR variants; it is mechanistically expected from hypothalamic mTORC1 nutrient sensing rather than incidental.
In a cohort of 28 individuals carrying nine pathogenic MTOR variants, sleep–wake disturbance emerged as a recognised feature alongside hyperphagia and hyperactivity.
notes: Recognised in a single cohort of 28 individuals carrying nine pathogenic MTOR variants, alongside hyperphagia and hyperactivity.

mechanism: Ser209-phosphorylated eIF4E promotes translation of Per1 mRNA in the SCN, converting a light pulse into a rise in PER protein and hence a phase shift
notes: Rests on a single report of light-regulated, eIF4E phosphorylation-dependent Per1 translation in the suprachiasmatic nucleus; not independently replicated.

mechanism: eIF4E-dependent translational control also governs Per2 protein output in the SCN, coupling translation-initiation state to the negative limb
notes: From a single report showing that eIF4E phosphorylation promotes translation of both Per1 and Per2 mRNAs in the suprachiasmatic nucleus; not independently replicated.

mechanism: 4E-BP1 restrains entrainment: Eif4ebp1-null mice show accelerated re-entrainment to a shifted light schedule and larger photic phase shifts, mirroring their elevated VIP levels
notes: Accelerated re-entrainment and larger light-induced phase shifts in 4E-BP1-null mice come from a single genetic study and have not been independently replicated.

mechanism: 4E-BP1 represses translation of Vip mRNA in SCN neurons; 4E-BP1 loss raises VIP levels, accelerating re-entrainment and increasing network synchrony.

notes: The documented sleep-to-mTOR arm. PMID 27117251: Tudor JC et al., Sci Signal 2016;9(425):ra41.

Bmal1-null tissues show constitutively elevated mTORC1 output, read out as increased S6K1 Thr389 phosphorylation and downstream S6 phosphorylation

SKS-associated MTOR variants reduced circadian reporter amplitude in engineered U2OS cells.

mTOR hyperactivation in the TSC-null model produces circadian behavioural abnormalities that are rescued by reducing Bmal1 gene dosage

Ageing produces thymic involution, contraction of the naive repertoire, accumulation of PD-1+ exhausted-like cells and the low-grade inflammation of inflammaging.
Age-associated decline in immune function is the premise of the three trials that define the geroprotective evidence base.

AKT retains mTORC1-independent output to MDM2, and thus to p53, one of several branches showing that mTORC1 is only one effector downstream of AKT.
Constitutively active AKT prevents denervation-induced atrophy in vivo.

Pharmacological mTOR inhibition induces autophagy and accelerates clearance of amyloid-beta in cellular and animal models.
Polyglutamine-expanded huntingtin is cleared by macroautophagy; rapamycin or CCI-779 reduces aggregates and improves outcomes in model organisms.
Suppressed autophagy is one of the two named mechanisms (with ER stress) through which chronic mTORC1 activation produces beta-cell dedifferentiation and failure.
Neural-specific deletion of Atg5 or Atg7 alone, with no disease mutant present, causes progressive motor deficits, ubiquitin-positive inclusions and neurodegeneration.
notes: Neurons cannot dilute damaged proteins by division, so basal flux carries more weight than in renewing tissue.

ATP-competitive pan-AKT inhibitor used in CAPItello-291.

The GATOR1-related familial focal epilepsies account for a substantial proportion of familial focal epilepsy and carry elevated risk of sudden unexpected death in epilepsy.

Hyperphagia and hyperactivity are recognised features in a cohort of 28 individuals with nine pathogenic MTOR variants, as hypothalamic nutrient sensing predicts.

Central hyperphagia is mechanistically expected from arcuate nucleus mTORC1 nutrient sensing rather than incidental.

mechanism: Epilepsy is a core feature of tuberous sclerosis complex alongside cortical tubers, SEGA, angiomyolipoma and LAM; refractory focal seizures are an approved everolimus indication.

4E-BP2 represses cap-dependent translation at the synapse: in its absence a single train that normally yields only early-phase potentiation induces late-phase LTP, so the induction threshold falls, yet late-phase LTP elicited by repeated high-frequency trains is impaired and hippocampus-dependent memory is deficient. Both excessive and deficient translational signalling are deleterious in brain.
notes: The lowered threshold for late-phase LTP in 4E-BP2-null hippocampus coexists with impaired late-phase LTP after strong stimulation and with deficient hippocampus-dependent memory.

42% of everolimus-treated patients achieved at least 50% angiomyolipoma reduction (EXIST-2).
context: tuberous sclerosis complex and sporadic LAM

mechanism: BOLERO-2 added everolimus to exemestane in HR-positive, HER2-negative advanced breast cancer progressing on an aromatase inhibitor, improving median PFS from 2.8 to 6.9 months by investigator assessment; overall survival 31.0 versus 26.6 months did not reach significance.
context: HR+/HER2- advanced breast cancer after aromatase inhibitor

mechanism: RADIANT-3 improved PFS from 4.6 to 11.0 months in advanced pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours and RADIANT-4 from 3.9 to 11.0 months in non-functional GI and lung NETs; the disease depends on secretory and translational programmes governed by 4E-BP and TOP mRNA control.
Approximately 35% of everolimus-treated patients achieved at least 50% SEGA volume reduction versus 0% on placebo (EXIST-1).

Everolimus is approved for TSC-associated SEGA, renal angiomyolipoma and refractory focal seizures on the basis of the EXIST programme; biallelic inactivation of a direct mTORC1 restraint in lesions driven by nothing else is the condition under which a rapalog does what its mechanism predicts.
PD-1+ CD4 and CD8 T cell fractions fell in the 218-participant everolimus vaccine-response trial, alongside the improvement in haemagglutination-inhibition titre.
context: adults aged 65 or older; 6 weeks before influenza vaccination
notes: Accumulation of PD-1+ exhausted-like cells is one of the defining features of immunosenescence.

Resistance exercise activates mTORC1 through phospholipase D-derived phosphatidic acid, mechanically induced membrane perturbation and focal adhesion signalling.
Nuclear FOXO1 drives gluconeogenic gene expression; it is inactivated by AKT once mTORC2 has phosphorylated AKT at Ser473.
Polyglutamine-expanded huntingtin aggregation drives Huntington's disease pathology.
IL-1alpha acts upstream of the IL1 receptor-NF-kB arm that sustains the SASP transcriptional programme.

Intracerebroventricular leucine raises hypothalamic S6K1 phosphorylation and suppresses food intake and body weight; rapamycin abolishes the effect.
notes: Established in rodents; unresolved in humans, where no study has separated central from peripheral contributions.

mechanism: The protein-feeding dose-response shifts rightward with age, so a per-meal leucine threshold of roughly 3-4 g is proposed to maximise synthesis in older adults.
notes: The per-meal leucine threshold is a practical proposal rather than an established requirement; a systematic review of postprandial post-exercise muscle protein synthesis found leucine dose to predict the response in older adults without identifying a discrete threshold.

context: human skeletal muscle, oral leucine bolus at rest

mechanism: MK2-dependent phosphorylation of the RNA-binding protein ZFP36L1 relieves degradation of SASP transcripts.

Deletion of mTOR in the adult mouse myocardium causes a fatal dilated cardiomyopathy with cardiomyocyte apoptosis and accumulation of 4E-BP1, marking the lower bound of the cardiac therapeutic window for mTOR inhibition.

mTOR signalling is required for oligodendrocyte differentiation and myelination. Bone requires mTOR signalling for osteoblast differentiation.

Deletion of mTOR in naive T cells favoured Foxp3-positive regulatory differentiation in the tested mouse model.

T cell-specific mTOR deletion abrogates Th1, Th2 and Th17 differentiation while promoting Foxp3+ regulatory T cell differentiation.
Adipocyte Raptor deletion impairs adipogenesis and reduces fat mass with enhanced mitochondrial respiration; the PPARgamma programme is the mTORC1 output of adipose tissue.
The PI3K-AKT-mTOR axis is the most frequently altered growth-promoting pathway in human cancer, with activating lesions in roughly 30-50% of tumours depending on type and sequencing depth.
Elevated mTORC1 activity contributes to cyst growth in polycystic kidney disease; trials were limited by dose-related toxicity rather than by absence of rationale.
Chronic mTORC1 hyperactivation drives beta-cell dedifferentiation and failure through ER stress and suppressed autophagy.

mTORC1 supports the glutaminolytic reprogramming that accompanies effector T-cell activation, alongside the glycolytic switch, acting through Myc-dependent glutaminase expression and increased glutamine anaplerosis.
mTOR signalling contributes to metabolic adaptation during T-cell activation; the contribution of this complex depends on lineage and stimulation conditions.

mechanism: mTOR-dependent dendritic translation underlies the late protein-synthesis-dependent phase of LTP; rapamycin blocks L-LTP while sparing the early phase.

mechanism: Microglial Tsc1 deletion is accompanied by astrocyte proliferation and severe early-onset spontaneous recurrent seizures, without a pro-inflammatory cytokine signature.
Chronic mTORC1 hyperactivation initially expands beta-cell mass and secretion but leads to dedifferentiation and failure through ER stress and suppressed autophagy.
Beta-cell-specific Raptor deletion impairs beta-cell mass and functional maturation.
Cardiac mTORC1 supports physiological hypertrophy, yet sustained activity contributes to maladaptive remodelling, which partial inhibition attenuates in multiple models.

Intracerebroventricular leucine raises hypothalamic S6K1 phosphorylation and suppresses food intake and body weight; rapamycin abolishes the effect.
notes: Established in rodents; no human study separates central from peripheral contribution.

mechanism: Chronic mTORC1 activation in obesity drives insulin resistance through S6K1-IRS-1 feedback and through lipotoxicity from constrained adipose storage capacity.
Reduced TOR signalling extends lifespan in Saccharomyces cerevisiae, Caenorhabditis elegans and Drosophila melanogaster, so TOR activity limits lifespan.

Sustained mTORC1 activity contributes to maladaptive cardiac remodelling, in contrast to the physiological hypertrophy the same complex supports, and partial inhibition attenuates pathological hypertrophy in several models.
notes: Cardiac mTOR also has protective roles, including after ischaemic injury, so the maladaptive arm is dose- and context-dependent rather than a uniform property of mTORC1 activity.

mechanism: Microglial Tsc1 loss produces an amoeboid, highly proliferative and phagocytic phenotype without a pro-inflammatory cytokine signature, with reduced synapse density.

Muscle-specific Raptor deletion produces progressive dystrophy, impaired oxidative capacity and shortened lifespan, so intact mTORC1 restrains the dystrophic phenotype; muscle-specific Rictor deletion is close to phenotypically silent.

Oligodendrocyte-lineage Raptor loss delays myelination onset and produces persistent hypomyelination with reduced sheath thickness, regionally worse in spinal cord.
notes: Established in rodents; effect of chronic low-dose inhibition on adult human white matter unresolved.

notes: Differentiation, expansion and suppressive function are distinct endpoints; mature Tregs require mTORC1 for normal function.

mTORC1-driven translation is required for the senescence-associated secretory phenotype, through IL1A and MAPKAPK2 translation.
Hepatic mTORC1 promotes SREBP1c processing and activity, driving the lipogenic programme of the liver.

Cardiac mTORC1 supports physiological hypertrophy; only the mTORC2 arm of the cardiomyocyte row was encoded.
In the arcuate nucleus mTORC1 operates as a nutrient sensor, which makes the hyperphagia of Smith-Kingsmore syndrome mechanistically expected rather than incidental.
notes: Established in rodents and unresolved in humans, where the central and peripheral contributions have not been separated; some metabolic effects attributed to liver, adipose tissue and beta-cells may therefore be centrally mediated.

mechanism: Podocyte Raptor deletion produces injury and proteinuria while Tsc1 deletion causes glomerulosclerosis: a calibrated rather than monotonic requirement.
Hepatic mTORC1 drives insulin-stimulated SREBP1c-dependent lipogenesis and restrains fasting ketogenesis.
notes: Activation of hepatic mTORC1 alone is not sufficient to drive lipogenesis: liver Tsc1 deletion lowers Akt signalling and protects against diet-induced steatosis, so Akt-dependent input is required alongside mTORC1.

mechanism: Pathway hyperactivation in the microglial compartment drives astrocyte proliferation and seizures, a non-neuronal contribution to the mTORopathies.

Oligodendrocyte-lineage Raptor loss delays onset of myelination and produces persistent hypomyelination with reduced sheath thickness, whereas Rictor loss has modest and largely transient effects; the requirement is regional, with spinal cord affected more than corpus callosum.
context: oligodendrocyte lineage; regional (spinal cord > corpus callosum)

mechanism: Rapidly renewing oral epithelium depends on mTORC1, which is why stomatitis affects roughly 30-60% of treated patients depending on indication and is substantially preventable with topical dexamethasone or tacrolimus prophylaxis.
Muscle-specific Raptor deletion produces progressive dystrophy, impaired oxidative capacity and shortened lifespan, establishing mTORC1 as the dominant complex in muscle.
Both complexes are required for the glycolytic and glutaminolytic reprogramming of effector T cell activation, so partial inhibition is the pharmacological objective.
Beta-cell Rictor deletion elevates p27, contributing to the imbalance between beta-cell proliferation and cell size.
Beta-cell Rictor deletion reduces AKT Ser473 phosphorylation and produces nuclear FOXO1 accumulation.

Adipocyte Rictor deletion reduces insulin-stimulated glucose uptake while altering lipid handling and body growth.

Adipose-tissue mTORC2 regulates ChREBP-driven de novo lipogenesis, with consequences for hepatic glucose metabolism.
Beta-cell Rictor deletion causes mild hyperglycaemia with reduced beta-cell mass, decreased AKT Ser473 phosphorylation, nuclear FOXO1 accumulation and elevated p27.
Adipose-specific Rictor deletion increases whole-body growth, so adipose mTORC2 negatively controls somatic growth.

Cardiomyocyte mTORC2 is cytoprotective in myocardial ischaemia through AKT-dependent anti-apoptotic signalling: loss of Rictor increases cardiomyocyte apoptosis and infarct damage, whereas shifting signalling from mTORC1 towards mTORC2 reduces it.

Loss of both mTOR complexes in CD4 T cells favours Foxp3+ regulatory T cell differentiation; an independent contribution of mTORC2 to this restraint, acting through AKT, is supported but less consistently than the mTORC1 arm.
context: de novo Treg differentiation in vitro; not mature Treg expansion
notes: Differentiation, expansion and suppressive function are distinct endpoints; mature Tregs require mTORC1 for normal function.
